edges.description: Motor-axon loss reduces muscle activation and produces acute flaccid limb weakness.
Failure of peripheral motor and sensory limbs of the reflex arc reduces or abolishes tendon reflexes.
Dorsal-root and sensory-nerve axonal loss produces objective sensory dysfunction.
Injured sensory fibers can generate tingling and other abnormal sensations.
Sensory-fiber and root injury can produce neuropathic, radicular, and musculoskeletal pain.
Severe cranial motor-nerve involvement can impair swallowing.
Severe motor-axon dysfunction can weaken respiratory muscles and require ventilatory support.
Involvement of autonomic peripheral fibers can produce cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and bladder dysfunction.

The preparation demonstrates antibody/complement deposition, ultrastructural injury, and motor-terminal conduction block while sparing postsynaptic membranes. It is a mechanistic motor-axon assay rather than a sensory-inclusive AMSAN model.

nodes.description: In a biologically defined subset of axonal GBS, sialylated C. jejuni lipooligosaccharides resemble peripheral-nerve gangliosides. The mimicry can initiate an antibody response that recognizes both bacterial carbohydrate and neural ganglioside. This mechanism is not asserted for every AMSAN case.

evidence.snippet: On sensitization with C. jejuni lipooligosaccharide, rabbits developed anti-GM1 IgG antibody and flaccid limb weakness.

evidence.reference_title: Guillain-Barre syndrome
evidence.snippet: preceding Campylobacter jejuni infection, molecular mimicry causes a cross-reactive antibody response to nerve gangliosides.

nodes.description: Antecedent C. jejuni enteritis is the best-defined trigger for the ganglioside-mimicry mechanism and is associated with motor and axonal GBS patterns. GBS-wide risk estimates must not be read as AMSAN-specific risk.

nodes.description: Activated B-cell and plasma-cell responses produce IgG against gangliosides such as GM1, GM1b, and GD1a. These antibodies occur in some, but not all, patients with axonal GBS. A small human study found the same antibody profile in AMSAN and AMAN, supporting a shared immune spectrum rather than a uniquely AMSAN-specific marker.

nodes.description: IVIG is one of two established immune treatments for GBS. The guideline regimen is 0.4 g/kg daily for five days, generally started within two weeks of weakness onset in a patient unable to walk unaided; selected patients may be treated at two to four weeks. Evidence and recommendations are GBS-wide, not AMSAN-specific.

evidence.reference_title: European Academy of Neurology/Peripheral Nerve Society Guideline on diagnosis and treatment of Guillain-Barre syndrome.
evidence.snippet: TF recommends intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) 0.4 g/kg for 5 days

nodes.description: Acute, usually symmetric, progressive flaccid weakness affects the legs and arms and may progress to inability to walk or complete paralysis.

evidence.snippet: progressive flaccid limb paresis and areflexia.

nodes.description: Macrophages accumulate around injured myelinated axons and can enter the periaxonal space. Human AMSAN autopsy establishes this localization, but the relative injurious versus debris-clearing role and timing remain uncertain.

nodes.description: Invasive ventilation is supportive therapy for respiratory failure. It does not modify the immune attack, so respiratory monitoring and timely airway planning remain essential.

nodes.description: Irreversible AMSAN injury is dominated by Wallerian-like degeneration and loss of motor and sensory fibers in ventral and dorsal roots and peripheral nerves. This acute pattern is not assumed to be length-dependent, and primary demyelination is not required.

nodes.description: Rehabilitation should begin during hospitalization and continue after discharge as needed. Physical and occupational therapy, graded mobility and strengthening, positioning and contracture prevention, speech/swallow care, respiratory therapy, assistive devices, and psychosocial support are tailored to weakness, sensory loss, fatigue, pain, and bulbar or respiratory deficits.

nodes.description: Neuropathic, radicular, and nociceptive pain should be assessed repeatedly and treated while accounting for respiratory and autonomic vulnerability. nodes.description: Plasma exchange is an established alternative first-line immune treatment for GBS. The guideline regimen is 12-15 L in four to five exchanges over one to two weeks, generally within four weeks of weakness onset when the patient cannot walk unaided. It is not routine rescue immediately after IVIG.
